# 1. Exploratory Data Analysis



```{r echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Import dataset
data <- read.csv2("euroleague_25_26.csv")
# Remove row number
data$No <- NULL
# Inspect data
#head(data)
#str(data)
#head(data)
```
The initial variable 'No', which served merely as a row index, was discarded from the data frame because it held no predictive or analytical value. Following this cleanup, the dataset consisted of r nrow(data) rows and r ncol(data) columns. Next, we split the variable 'Min' using strsplit(data$Min, ":") to extract the minutes and converted them into a numeric variable. We set the player names as row labels so we could identify individuals directly in the PCA and MDS plots, using make.unique() as a safeguard against duplicate names. We then removed the 'PLAYER' and 'Min' columns because they were rendered redundant by the new row labels and the numeric minutes variable. Finally, we retained only the players who played for at least 5 minutes and participated in 5 or more games. The averages of players with very little playing time are highly unstable and could distort the subsequent analysis. After this filtering step, 60 of the original 71 players remained in the dataset.


```{r echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Split minutes
aux <- strsplit(data$Min, ":")

# Extract minutes and convert to numeric
data$`Min 2` <- as.numeric(sapply(aux, `[`, 1))

# Inspect result
#head(data[, c("Min", "Min 2")])

```

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Assign player names as row labels
rownames(data) <- make.unique(as.character(data$PLAYER))

# Remove PLAYER and Min columns
data$PLAYER <- NULL
data$Min <- NULL

# Inspect result
#head(data)
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Number of players before filtering
nrow(data)

# Keep players with at least 5 minutes and 5 games
data <- data[data$`Min 2` >= 5 & data$GP >= 5, ]

# Number of players after filtering
#nrow(data)

# Inspect result
#head(data)
```

# 2. Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

## 2a
We ran PCA on all numerical variables, standardised (scale.unit = TRUE). Standardising was necessary because the variables are on different scales: percentages, counts, and minutes. We included TEAM and POSITION as supplementary qualitative variables and PIR as a supplementary quantitative variable. They do not influence the construction of the components but are projected onto them afterwards to help interpretation. We excluded PIR from the active variables because it is itself a composite of the other statistics.

```{r echo=FALSE}
#install.packages("FactoMineR")

library(FactoMineR)

# Convert categorical variables to factors
data$TEAM <- as.factor(data$TEAM)
data$POSITION <- as.factor(data$POSITION)

# Identify supplementary variables
quali_vars <- which(names(data) %in% c("TEAM", "POSITION"))
quanti_vars <- which(names(data) == "PIR")

# Apply PCA
pca <- PCA(
  data,
  scale.unit = TRUE,
  quali.sup = quali_vars,
  quanti.sup = quanti_vars,
  graph = FALSE
)

# Inspect PCA results
summary(pca)
```

## 2b. Number of Principal Components

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Display eigenvalues and explained variance
pca$eig

# Number of components with eigenvalue > 1
sum(pca$eig[, 1] > 1)

# Scree plot
barplot(
  pca$eig[, 1],
  names.arg = paste0("PC", 1:nrow(pca$eig)),
  xlab = "Principal Components",
  ylab = "Eigenvalue",
  main = "Scree Plot",
  col = "steelblue"
)

abline(h = 1, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

Based on the Kaiser criterion, four principal components should be retained, as their eigenvalues exceed 1. The scree plot shows a particularly steep decline after PC2, indicating that the first two components explain most of the variance (cumulative 58,58%). However, we retain the first 3 PCs (PC3 explaining 7,7% of variance), explaining a cumulative variance of 66,34%, since PC3 brings valuable information to the analysis by capturing the relationship between three-point shooting vs. physical play that we explain further in the following questions.

## 2c

The variable plots show the correlation of each active variable with the principal components. Longer arrows indicate variables that are better represented in the plane shown. PIR appears as a dashed supplementary arrow.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.show='hold', out.width='49%', fig.width=5, fig.height=4}
# 2c. PCA Variable Plots

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(pca, choix = "var", axes = c(1, 2))
plot(pca, choix = "var", axes = c(2, 3))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Variable coordinates and correlations
pca$var$coord
pca$var$cor

# Contributions of variables
pca$var$contrib

# PC1 vs. PC2
plot(pca, choix = "var", axes = c(1, 2))

# PC2 vs. PC3
plot(pca, choix = "var", axes = c(2, 3))
```

## 2d

**PC1 (39.30%) – Overall Player Activity:** Most statistical variables are positively correlated with PC1, particularly points, minutes played, and rebounds. This dimension represents overall player activity and statistical contribution.

**PC2 (19.28%) – Playmaking vs. Rebounding:** Assists, turnovers, and steals correlate positively with PC2, while rebounds and blocks correlate negatively. This dimension distinguishes playmaking-oriented players from inside players.

**PC3 (7.76%) – Three-Point Shooting vs. Physical Play:** Three-point shooting percentage and games played correlate positively with PC3, while blocks against and turnovers correlate negatively. This dimension may reflect differences in playing style, although its interpretation is less clear.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, out.width="60%"}
# 2e. PCA Individual Plots

# PC1 vs. PC2
plot(pca, choix = "ind", axes = c(1, 2))

# PC2 vs. PC3
plot(pca, choix = "ind", axes = c(2, 3))
```

The PC1–PC2 plot (58.58% explained variance) separates players mainly by overall statistical activity (PC1) and playing style (PC2). Players 33 and 14 show high PC1 scores, while player 44 has a low score. PC2 distinguishes playmaking-oriented players, such as player 24, from more inside-oriented players, such as players 33 and 17.

The PC2–PC3 plot (27.04% explained variance) highlights additional differences in playing style, particularly three-point shooting. Players 25 and 23 have relatively high PC3 scores. Player positions partly reflect their roles, with guards tending towards higher PC2 values and centers towards lower values. However, the teams overlap considerably, indicating no clear separation by team.

# 3. Multidimensional Scaling (MDS)

## 3a. Metric MDS - Euclidean Distance


We applied classical (metric) MDS to the Euclidean distance matrix of the standardised numerical variables (PIR excluded, as in PCA). Classical MDS on Euclidean distances of standardised data gives the same configuration as the PCA individual map, so the Euclidean MDS plot is essentially the PCA PC1–PC2 individual plot, labelled with player names.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=7}

# Select active numerical variables (exclude PIR)
numerical_data <- data[, sapply(data, is.numeric)]
numerical_data$PIR <- NULL

# Calculate Euclidean distances on scaled data
d_eu <- dist(scale(numerical_data))

# Apply metric MDS
mds_eu <- cmdscale(d_eu, eig = TRUE)

# Plot the first two coordinates
x <- mds_eu$points[, 1]
y <- mds_eu$points[, 2]

plot(x, y,
     xlab = "Coordinate 1",
     ylab = "Coordinate 2",
     main = "Metric MDS - Euclidean Distance",
     type = "n",
     xlim = range(x) + c(-1, 1),
     ylim = range(y) + c(-1, 1))

text(x, y, labels = rownames(data), cex = 0.5)
```

## 3b
The Euclidean MDS plot shows a central concentration of players with relatively similar statistical profiles, without clearly separated clusters. Some players, such as Walter Tavares, Nikola Milutinov, and Facundo Campazzo, occupy more isolated positions, indicating distinct playing characteristics. Overall, the plot reveals both similarities among many players and substantial differences for certain individuals.

## 3c. Metric MDS - Gower Distance


We used Gower distance because it can combine numerical variables with the categorical variable POSITION. Each variable contributes a dissimilarity between 0 and 1: range-scaled absolute differences for numerical variables, and simple mismatch for categorical ones. We then applied Metric MDS to the resulting distance matrix. The first two coordinates explain 57,63% of the total variation.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=7}

library(cluster)

# Select numerical variables and POSITION
gower_data <- data[, c(names(numerical_data), "POSITION")]

# Ensure POSITION is categorical
gower_data$POSITION <- as.factor(gower_data$POSITION)

# Calculate Gower distances
d_gower <- daisy(gower_data, metric = "gower")

# Apply metric MDS
mds_gower <- cmdscale(d_gower, eig = TRUE)

# Plot the first two coordinates
x <- mds_gower$points[, 1]
y <- mds_gower$points[, 2]

plot(x, y,
     xlab = "Coordinate 1",
     ylab = "Coordinate 2",
     main = "Metric MDS - Gower Distance",
     type = "n")

text(x, y, labels = rownames(data), cex = 0.5)

# Eigenvalues and goodness of fit
mds_gower$eig
mds_gower$GOF
```
# 3d. Interpretation of Gower MDS Dimensions
```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=15, fig.height=8}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# MDS coordinates
x <- mds_gower$points[, 1]
y <- mds_gower$points[, 2]

# Plot by POSITION
plot(x, y, type = "n",
     xlab = "Coordinate 1", ylab = "Coordinate 2",
     main = "Gower MDS - Player Positions")

text(x, y, labels = data$POSITION,
     col = as.numeric(as.factor(data$POSITION)),
     cex = 0.7)

# Plot by TEAM
plot(x, y, type = "n",
     xlab = "Coordinate 1", ylab = "Coordinate 2",
     main = "Gower MDS - Teams")

text(x, y, labels = data$TEAM,
     col = as.numeric(as.factor(data$TEAM)),
     cex = 0.7)

# Plot by PTS
plot(x, y, type = "n",
     xlab = "Coordinate 1", ylab = "Coordinate 2",
     main = "Gower MDS - Points")

text(x, y, labels = round(data$PTS, 1),
     cex = 0.7)

# Plot by AST
plot(x, y, type = "n",
     xlab = "Coordinate 1", ylab = "Coordinate 2",
     main = "Gower MDS - Assists")

text(x, y, labels = round(data$AST, 1),
     cex = 0.7)
```
**Coordinate 1 – Scoring Activity:** Players with higher average points generally appear on the left, while lower-scoring players tend to appear on the right, suggesting that this dimension partly reflects scoring activity.

**Coordinate 2 – Playing Position and Playmaking:** Centers are mainly located at positive values, guards at negative values, and forwards in between. Higher assist averages also tend to occur at negative values, indicating that this dimension distinguishes inside-oriented players from playmakers.

**Team Membership:** Players from all four teams overlap considerably, suggesting that team membership does not strongly explain the MDS dimensions.

## 3e
Gower MDS provides clearer grouping of players by position, with centers, guards, and forwards showing a more distinct separation. This is because Gower distance incorporates the categorical variable POSITION alongside numerical statistics. Euclidean MDS mainly reflects differences in numerical performance and shows less distinct groups.
# 4. Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA)

We converted each numerical variable into a two-level factor: “Over average” if the player’s value exceeds the variable mean, and “Below average” otherwise. This way we are able to analyse the continuous statistics together with TEAM and POSITION in MCA. The trade-off was a loss of information, since we discard the magnitude of differences within each category.

# 4a. Convert Numerical Variables to Binary Categories
```{r echo=FALSE}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Create MCA dataset
mca_data <- data

# Identify numerical variables
num_vars <- sapply(mca_data, is.numeric)

# Convert numerical variables to binary factors
mca_data[num_vars] <- lapply(mca_data[num_vars], function(x) {
  factor(
    ifelse(x > mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
           "Over average", "Below average")
  )
})

# Ensure categorical variables are factors
mca_data$TEAM <- as.factor(mca_data$TEAM)
mca_data$POSITION <- as.factor(mca_data$POSITION)

# Inspect results
str(mca_data)
summary(mca_data)
```


# 4b. Multiple Correspondence Analysis
```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=3}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

library(FactoMineR)

# Apply MCA
mca <- MCA(mca_data, graph = FALSE)

# Inspect MCA results
summary(mca)
mca$eig

# Describe dimensions
dimdesc(mca)

# Scree plot
barplot(mca$eig[, 2],
        main = "MCA - Explained Inertia",
        xlab = "Dimensions",
        ylab = "Percentage of Inertia")

# Plot categories
plot(mca, choix = "var", axes = c(1, 2))

# MCA Category Map
plot(mca, invisible = "ind",
     title = "MCA - Categories")

# Plot individuals
plot(mca, choix = "ind", axes = c(1, 2),
     label = "none")
```

The first two MCA dimensions explain **42.08% of the total inertia** (25.46% and 16.62%).

**Dimension 1 – Overall Statistical Involvement:** This dimension is mainly associated with minutes played (R² = 0.750), PIR (R² = 0.748), and points scored (R² = 0.564). Above-average performance categories are located on the positive side, while below-average categories appear on the negative side.

**Dimension 2 – Inside Play vs. Playmaking:** Playing position (R² = 0.580), offensive rebounds (R² = 0.555), and assists (R² = 0.377) strongly characterize this dimension. Centers and above-average rebounding categories are located at positive values, while guards and above-average assists appear at negative values.

The individual factor map shows differences in player profiles without clearly separated clusters. Team categories are located near the origin, suggesting little influence on the first two dimensions. However, Dimension 3 (6.88%) is strongly associated with team membership (R² = 0.719).

## 4c
All three methods reveal similar patterns. PCA and MCA identify overall statistical involvement as the first dimension and differences between playmaking and inside-oriented players as the second. Euclidean MDS highlights differences in numerical player statistics, while Gower MDS provides clearer separation by playing position. Unlike PCA, MCA uses categorized performance variables, resulting in some information loss but making above- and below-average performance profiles easier to interpret.
